questions.question: Problem 122: During much of the powered phase of the maximum altitude flight, Joe Walker maintained the X-15 at a climb angle of 32 degrees. When the rocket propellants ran out, the X-15 was climbing through 176,000 feet at a flight velocity of 5600 ft/s. Calculate the rate-of-climb at the time of engine burnout.
questions.explanation:
Given: During much of the powered phase of the maximum altitude flight, Joe Walker maintained the X-15 at a climb angle of 32 degrees. When the rocket propellants ran out, the X-15 was climbing through 176,000 feet at a flight velocity of 5600 ft/s. Calculate the rate-of-climb at the time of engine burnout.

Formula: Rate of climb is the vertical component of velocity: ROC = V*sin(gamma).

Solution: Convert the supplied quantities to a consistent unit system, substitute them into the formula above, and solve for the requested quantity. For multiple requested parts, repeat the calculation for each part. This gives 2968 fps.

questions.question: Problem 123: The thrust of the XLR 99 rocket engine was essentially constant at 57,000 lb during the powered phase of the X-15 flight. The empty weight of the X-15 was 14,590 lb. Calculate the rate-of-climb of the X-15.
questions.explanation:

Formula: Rate of climb from excess power is ROC = (T-D)*V/W. Use the flight velocity stated for the burnout condition and convert the result to ft/s.

questions.question: Problem 124: T he maximum lift-to-drag ratio for the CP-1 is 13.6. Calculate the minimum glide angle and the maximum range measured along the ground covered by the CP-1 in a power-off glide that starts at an altitude of 10,000 ft.

Formula: For a power-off glide, tan(gamma) = D/L = 1/(L/D). Ground range R = h/tan(gamma), assuming still air and no turns.

Solution: Convert the supplied quantities to a consistent unit system, substitute them into the formula above, and solve for the requested quantity. For multiple requested parts, repeat the calculation for each part. This gives 4.2 °, 25.6 mile.
